:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Consider the triangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(0,0), (1,1)$ and $(-1,1),$ traversed counterclockwise, and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ Express $\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}x\sin{y}\,\mathrm{d}x+ (x^2\cos{y}-y^2)\,\mathrm{d}y}$ as a repeated integral.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/2f/2fa3c84359cec5f5e0750552e5a4b24b20b8dbc3d65b909aea908e1505cfb5e3.png)

We have that $P(x,y)= x\sin{y}$ and $Q(x,y)= x^2\cos{y}-y^2.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D = \{(x,y) :  -y\leq x\leq y,\, 0\leq y \leq 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dx+({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y}^{y}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Consider the triangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(0,0),(1,0)$ and $(1,2),$ traversed counterclockwise, and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ Express ${∮}_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+2{x}^{2}y\,dy$ as a repeated integral.

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/2e/2e63a57e50b60d7f0c6a3ce12d164716e2cba71c6bd4c6df10460a35beba4209.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 2x}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+2{x}^{2}y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4xy-2xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2x}2xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

D=\{(x,y):-2\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx+(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Consider the closed curve $C,$ which is the boundary of the region enclosed by $y=1-{x}^{2}$ and $y=0.$ Express ${∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-y)\,dx+(2x-{y}^{2})\,dy$ as a repeated integral.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/a3/a3fe0bbc283a2eaacffad4b6be071f601781b6b77b2df0dd9b30abb22653c738.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}-y$ and $Q(x,y)=2x-{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 1-{x}^{2}\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-y)\,dx+(2x-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-(-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$
